how_categories_were_assigned: by `categories.categories_of` at sampling time, before annotation. Where a span carries a broad and a narrow label the narrow one is reported, so the table partitions the spans rather than double-counting the hierarchy.
modified_means: the span carries at least one of the four modifiers — the UNION of the dimension columns. `label_instances` is their sum and `multi_label_spans` the difference, so the inclusion-exclusion is checkable per row: dimensions co-occur, and `no history of X` is negated AND historical. Its complement, `unmodified`, is what ConText and this codebase call `affirmed`.
publishable: counts only. Surfaces, sentences and note ids stay in data/; the categories are derived from UMLS semantic types, which are identifiers rather than licensed strings.
question: What kind of concept carries each assertion in the gold?
why: A pooled per-dimension F1 treats every span as interchangeable. A disease and a medication are qualified by different constructions, so the mix of concepts in a gold determines what its numbers mean. This states the mix.
why_not_non_affirmed: because it is false for two of the four. `historical` does not withhold the assertion — `history of hypertension` AFFIRMS the hypertension and locates it in the past; `family` affirms the finding in someone else. Only `negated` truly withholds, and `uncertain` only partly. `non-affirmed` is accurate only with the trailing qualifier `about the patient now`, which drops off every time the term is used alone. Each dimension MODIFIES the asserted presence of the concept, which is what the SEMANTIC operators flip, so `modifier` is both positively defined and true of all four.
why_not_positive: it inverts between frames. Clinically, `positive for pneumonia` means the patient has it — an UNMODIFIED span here. In the scorer, `gold_positives` for `negated` counts spans that ARE negated, which is clinically negative. `modified`/`unmodified` describes what the note does to the concept and does not flip between those readings.
